Lest
lest
conj. (of negative purpose; rendering Hebrew pen, Greek me pos and hina me)
From Saxon þy læs þe, by the less that — worn down to lest. It introduces the thing to be avoided, and so is the particle of every warning in Scripture: the danger named so that it may be escaped.

Biblical Definition

Lest introduces what must not happen, and it is therefore the grammar of warning. It appears in Eve's report of the prohibition — “neither shall ye touch it, lest ye die” (Genesis 3:3) — and in Moses' charge against the peculiar danger of prosperity: “Then beware lest thou forget the LORD, which brought thee forth out of the land of Egypt” (Deuteronomy 6:12). That warning is given precisely at the point where Israel is promised great and goodly cities she did not build; comfort, not hardship, is the setting for forgetting God. Agur asks for neither poverty nor riches with the same particle governing both halves: “Lest I be full, and deny thee, and say, Who is the LORD? or lest I be poor, and steal, and take the name of my God in vain” (Proverbs 30:9). Christ commands watchfulness in Gethsemane with it: “Watch ye and pray, lest ye enter into temptation” (Mark 14:38). And Paul uses it for the danger of discipline pressed too far, urging the Corinthians to forgive a repentant offender “lest perhaps such a one should be swallowed up with overmuch sorrow” (2 Corinthians 2:7).

Webster 1828 Definition

A conjunction introducing what is to be prevented or avoided; that not, for fear that. In Scripture it is the particle of warning — beware lest thou forget, watch and pray lest ye enter into temptation.

expand to see more

LEST, conj. [Sax. þy læs þe, by the less that.] That not; for fear that.

2. It introduces a clause expressing something to be prevented; as, take heed lest ye fall.

3. It governs the subjunctive mood, the event being contingent and undesired.

4. It answers to the Hebrew pen and the Greek me pos.

5. In Scripture, beware lest thou forget the LORD, Deut. 6; Watch ye and pray, lest ye enter into temptation, Mark 14.

Key Scripture

Genesis 3:3 — "But of the fruit of the tree which is in the midst of the garden, God hath said, Ye shall not eat of it, neither shall ye touch it, lest ye die."

Deuteronomy 6:12 — "Then beware lest thou forget the LORD, which brought thee forth out of the land of Egypt, from the house of bondage."

Proverbs 30:9 — "Lest I be full, and deny thee, and say, Who is the LORD? or lest I be poor, and steal, and take the name of my God in vain."

Mark 14:38 — "Watch ye and pray, lest ye enter into temptation. The spirit truly is ready, but the flesh is weak."

Modern Corruption

Warning has fallen out of favour as a mode of Christian address, treated as fear-mongering or as inconsistent with assurance. Scripture warns constantly, and warns the saints most of all; the warnings are among the means by which God keeps His people.

expand to see more

The objection runs that if the elect cannot finally fall away, warnings to them are empty threats. The Reformed answer is that God ordains means as well as ends, and the warnings are among the means. Hebrews is addressed to professing Christians and is full of lest: lest any of you be hardened through the deceitfulness of sin, lest any man fall after the same example of unbelief. These are not idle. The believer who reads them and takes heed is being kept by them, and the man who dismisses them as inapplicable to himself has already shown the disposition they were written against.

Deuteronomy 6:12 identifies the direction from which the danger usually comes, and it is not persecution. Israel is warned about forgetting God at the exact moment she is given houses full of good things she did not fill. Prosperity is the more dangerous climate because nothing in it announces itself as a trial. Agur's prayer is the wise man's response — asking to be spared both extremities, since riches tempt to denial and want tempts to theft. A church in comfortable circumstances that has stopped hearing warnings is in the precise condition Moses feared.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew pen introduces the undesired contingency; Greek uses me pos and hina me with the subjunctive. The particle always governs an event to be avoided, never one intended.

expand to see more

Hebrew pen (H6435) — lest, that not, peradventure; the standard particle of negative purpose.

Greek hina me (G2443, G3361) — that not, lest; purpose clause with the negative.

Greek me pos (G3381) — lest by any means, lest perhaps; used where the danger is uncertain but real.

Hebrew shakach (H7911) — to forget; the specific danger of Deuteronomy 6:12.

Greek peirasmos (G3986) — temptation, trial, testing; what the disciples were to watch and pray against.

Usage

"Of the danger attending prosperity: beware lest thou forget the LORD, which brought thee forth out of the land of Egypt (Deuteronomy 6:12)."

"Of both riches and poverty as temptations: Lest I be full, and deny thee... or lest I be poor, and steal (Proverbs 30:9)."

"Of watchfulness commanded in the garden: Watch ye and pray, lest ye enter into temptation (Mark 14:38)."
